ns1:channel.ns1:title: Communications Earth & Environment
ns1:channel.ns1:description:
Communications Earth & Environment is an open access journal from Nature Portfolio that publishes high-quality research, reviews and commentary in the Earth, environmental and planetary sciences. The papers we publish represent significant advances that bring new insight to a specialized area of research. We also provide a community forum for issues of importance to Earth, environmental and planetary scientists, regardless of sub-discipline.

Our scope covers all areas of the geosciences, climate and environmental sciences as well as planetary sciences, including those at the interface with ecology, sustainability and environmental social sciences. Primary research of interest to the journal includes important insights gained from field work, novel analyses of existing data, numerical or analytical modelling, theoretical studies or laboratory experiments.

We encourage submissions that provide independent confirmation of particularly influential publications.

The submission and review processes are managed by our in-house professional editors supported by our Editorial Board Members, who provide technical expertise across the breadth of the Earth, environmental and planetary sciences. We are committed to rapid dissemination of important research results. Articles are published on a continuous basis to ensure swift communication of findings.

ns1:item.ns1:title: Diffusional earthquakes and their slip-distance scaling
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 10 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-04043-4

A scaling relation unifying diffusional earthquakes is derived from prolonged natural earthquake swarms in Northeast Japan and a compilation of cataloged slow earthquakes, injection-induced seismicity, and natural earthquake swarms, with earthquake magnitude constrained by diffusive envelopes.
ns1:item.dc:title: Diffusional earthquakes and their slip-distance scaling
ns1:item.dc:creator: Dye SK Sato
Keisuke Yoshida
ns1:item.dc:source: Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 2026-09-10; | doi:10.1038/s43247-026-04043-4

ns1:item.ns1:title: Nickel isotopes reveal micrometeorite accretion on the lunar farside dominated by inner Solar System materials
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 10 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-04038-1

Material accreted to the Moon over time through impactors has dominantly originated from the inner solar system, according to analysis of Ni isotopic compositions in regolith samples and lithic clasts returned from the lunar farside by the Chang’e 6 mission

ns1:item.ns1:title: Atmospheric aridity drives functional reorganisation and resilience loss in global forests
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 10 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-04040-7

Over one-third of global forests are becoming simultaneously more productive and less resilient, with rising atmospheric dryness driving resilience loss and reshaping how forests coordinate carbon uptake and water use, according to analyses of 20 years of remote sensing data.
ns1:item.dc:title: Atmospheric aridity drives functional reorganisation and resilience loss in global forests

ns1:item.ns1:title: REE-depleted anatectic marble reveals the primary source of crustal carbonatites
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 10 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-04048-z

Granulite-facies metacarbonate melting generates carbonatitic melts with ~35% REE enrichment, highlighting crustal carbonate melting as a key mechanism for rare-earth elements redistribution in orogenic crust, according to analysis of a 15-m thick marble layer exposed in the Serre Massif of Calabria in southern Italy.
ns1:item.dc:title: REE-depleted anatectic marble reveals the primary source of crustal carbonatites

ns1:item.ns1:title: Rapid increase of climate extremes reveals new areas of concern in Amazonia
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 10 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-03975-1

Climate change impacts in the Amazon, particularly heat and drought extremes, are increasing faster than average climate trends, with especially rapid changes in the central-northern region that has so far attracted less attention than other regions.
ns1:item.dc:title: Rapid increase of climate extremes reveals new areas of concern in Amazonia

ns1:item.ns1:title: The active Bengal lobe complex as the modern terminal sink of Earth’s largest submarine fan
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 10 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-04037-2

“The currently active lobe complex and modern sediment sink of the Bengal Fan are constrained to the middle fan, where an avulsion of the active channel shifted its location 1,800 km landward, establishing a critical closure point for the world’s largest source-to-sink system”
ns1:item.dc:title: The active Bengal lobe complex as the modern terminal sink of Earth’s largest submarine fan

ns1:item.ns1:title: Growth rate of the preserved Antarctic continent reveals the anatomy of a late developer
ns1:item.content:encoded:
Communications Earth & Environment, Published online: 10 September 2026; doi:10.1038/s43247-026-04024-7

“Primary growth of the Antarctic continent occurred a billion years later than other well-studied continents, since Archean crust is found to be rare beneath Antarctica’s ice sheet, as shown by offshore detrital zircon analyses”.
ns1:item.dc:title: Growth rate of the preserved Antarctic continent reveals the anatomy of a late developer
